title: Maximum Likelihood Estimation: Build the Likelihood, Find the Maximum
breadcrumb: Statistical Inference → Point Estimation → Maximum likelihood
engineName: Estimation and inference — let the observed data decide which parameter value makes them most plausible
provenance: New foundational lesson authored on 15 November 2026 to fill the missing learner-facing lesson_t4.json identified during the independent Statistical Inference audit. Scope is the UGC NET Statistics Paper 2 Unit IV topic 'maximum likelihood estimators', with links to sufficiency and Fisher information. The existing inference_t4_mastery pool is reused; no question-bank records are altered. Numerical examples and derivatives are derived in this lesson and should be checked by the repository validators before release.
objectives: Distinguish a likelihood function from a probability distribution for the parameter.
Construct a likelihood and log-likelihood for an iid sample.
Find an MLE by differentiation when the maximum is an interior point, and check endpoints and parameter restrictions.
Use the invariance property to estimate a function of the parameter.
Recognise boundary MLEs when the support depends on the parameter.
Explain why an MLE need not be unbiased and state the usual large-sample qualifications.

prereq.name: Probability mass functions and densities
prereq.why: The likelihood starts with the model's pmf or density. You must be able to identify which expression is evaluated at each observation.

prereq.name: Logarithms and differentiation
prereq.why: For most continuous parameter models, the score is the derivative of the log-likelihood. Practise differentiating log θ and log(1−θ).

prereq.name: Sufficiency and factorisation
prereq.why: The likelihood and sufficient statistic are closely connected. The MLE is often a function of a sufficient statistic, but the ideas are not identical.

sheet: Likelihood: L(θ;x) = ∏ᵢ f(xᵢ;θ) for an iid sample. The observations are fixed; θ varies.
Log-likelihood: ℓ(θ) = log L(θ) = Σᵢ log f(xᵢ;θ). Maximising ℓ gives the same maximiser as maximising L.
Interior candidate: solve U(θ) = dℓ/dθ = 0, then check it is a maximum and lies in the parameter space.
Never stop at the score equation: also inspect boundaries, support restrictions and whether a maximum exists.
Invariance: if θ̂ maximises L(θ), then g(θ̂) maximises the induced likelihood for ψ = g(θ), under the usual MLE convention.
Bernoulli(p): p̂ = x̄. Poisson(λ): λ̂ = x̄. Exponential(rate λ): λ̂ = 1/x̄.
Normal with μ and σ² both unknown: μ̂ = x̄ and σ̂² = Σ(Xᵢ−x̄)²/n. The unbiased sample variance uses n−1.
Uniform(0,θ): L(θ) = θ⁻ⁿ I(θ ≥ X₍ₙ₎); the MLE is X₍ₙ₎, found at the boundary, not from an interior score root.
MLEs are not generally unbiased. Consistency and asymptotic normality require suitable regularity conditions.
A likelihood is not a probability distribution over θ; it need not integrate or sum to one over the parameter space.
cards: What is held fixed in a likelihood?
The observed data are fixed. The likelihood is viewed as a function of the unknown parameter.
The log changes products into sums and is strictly increasing, so it preserves the maximiser.
U(θ) = dℓ(θ)/dθ. An interior differentiable maximum must have score zero, but a zero score alone does not prove a maximum.
For ψ = g(θ), the MLE is g(θ̂), provided the MLE convention and induced parameterisation are used.
Why can the MLE be biased?
Maximum likelihood maximises the observed likelihood; it does not impose E[θ̂] = θ. For example, the exponential rate MLE n/ΣXᵢ has positive finite-sample bias.
What if the support depends on θ?
Check the feasible region before differentiating. For U(0,θ), the likelihood is maximised at θ̂ = X₍ₙ₎.
traps: Treating L(θ) as a probability density for θ. It is not a posterior distribution.
Differentiating L when log L is shorter, or forgetting that log preserves the maximiser.
Accepting a stationary point without checking the second derivative, endpoints and parameter space.
Using an interior score equation when the support itself depends on θ.
Confusing the normal MLE of σ² (divide by n) with the unbiased sample variance (divide by n−1).
Assuming every MLE is unbiased or that every model has a unique finite MLE.

tricks.why: The support may depend on θ. If it does, the maximum may sit at a boundary and the score equation can miss it.
For iid data take logs immediately: ℓ(θ) = Σ log f(xᵢ;θ).
If it asks for g(θ), transform the MLE; do not accidentally report the estimate of θ itself.
Likelihood maximisation for normal σ² gives divisor n. The n−1 estimator is the unbiased correction.

shortcuts: Bernoulli: p̂ = x̄; Poisson: λ̂ = x̄; Exponential(rate): λ̂ = 1/x̄.
Normal(μ,σ²), both unknown: μ̂ = x̄ and σ̂² = Σ(Xᵢ−x̄)²/n.
Uniform(0,θ): θ̂ = X₍ₙ₎. Check the support boundary before differentiating.
For ψ = g(θ), use ψ̂ = g(θ̂) under MLE invariance.
remember: Likelihood is a function of the parameter for the observed sample; it is not a probability distribution over the parameter.
Score zero gives a candidate, not a certificate. Check the whole parameter space.
MLE does not mean unbiased estimator.

traps: The likelihood is not a probability distribution over the parameter.
A score equation is only an interior candidate condition.
The normal variance MLE uses n, not n−1.
A parameter-dependent support often produces a boundary MLE.
Invariance estimates g(θ), not the derivative g′(θ).

scenes.title: Before the lesson — four tools to have ready
scenes.objective: Refresh the small amount of probability and calculus needed to build a likelihood.
body: Maximum likelihood sounds more complicated than it is. The central task is simple: write down how likely the observed data are under a proposed parameter value, then choose the value that makes that likelihood largest.
The algebra uses products, logarithms and derivatives. This short check makes sure those are not the things slowing you down.

items.ask: For an iid sample, how do you write the joint density or pmf?
items.recall: Multiply the individual contributions: f(x₁;θ)f(x₂;θ)…f(xₙ;θ) = ∏ᵢ f(xᵢ;θ).
refresh: Independence is why the product appears. If observations are not independent, do not automatically use this product; write the correct joint model.
The same product rule works for discrete pmfs and continuous densities.

items.ask: What is log(ab), and what is log(aⁿ)?
items.recall: log(ab) = log a + log b; log(aⁿ) = n log a.
refresh: These two rules turn a product likelihood into a sum and pull repeated factors outside the sum.

items.ask: What must be true at an interior differentiable maximum?
items.recall: The first derivative is zero. It is a necessary condition, not a sufficient one.
refresh: A stationary point can be a maximum, a minimum or a saddle/flat point. You still need to check its nature and compare boundaries.

items.ask: What is the difference between a parameter space and the sample space?
items.recall: The sample space contains possible data; the parameter space contains allowed values of the unknown parameter.
refresh: For a Bernoulli probability, the parameter space is 0 ≤ p ≤ 1. An algebraic answer outside it is not an admissible estimate.

scenes.title: The model asks a question; the data answer it
body: Suppose a coin is tossed ten times and the observed sequence contains seven heads. Consider three possible values for the probability of heads: 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8. Which value makes the observed result most plausible?

The likelihood compares those parameter values using the data already observed. It does not ask for the probability that the parameter equals 0.8. It asks how well each proposed parameter value explains the sample.
Maximum likelihood chooses the parameter value at which this comparison is largest. The data are fixed throughout; only the proposed parameter changes.

aside.body: Probability: fix θ and ask how likely the data are. Likelihood: fix the observed data and compare the values of θ. The numerical expression may be the same, but the question being asked is different.

ask.q: If a likelihood value is larger at θ = 0.8 than at θ = 0.5, what can you conclude?
ask.nudge: For this observed sample, θ = 0.8 gives the larger likelihood. It does not mean the probability that θ = 0.8 is larger.

scenes.title: Build the likelihood and take its logarithm
scenes.objective: Write the likelihood correctly and obtain the score equation.

blocks.body: For independent observations X₁,…,Xₙ with common pmf or density f(x;θ), the likelihood is L(θ;x) = ∏ᵢ₌₁ⁿ f(xᵢ;θ). The observed values x₁,…,xₙ are held fixed.

blocks.h: The likelihood is not a distribution for θ
blocks.body: A likelihood is not required to sum or integrate to one over θ. A Bayesian posterior is a probability distribution for θ after combining a likelihood with a prior; the likelihood alone is not.
ℓ(θ) = log L(θ) = Σᵢ₌₁ⁿ log f(xᵢ;θ). Because log is strictly increasing, L and ℓ have the same maximiser. The log is usually easier to differentiate.
U(θ) = dℓ(θ)/dθ. If the maximum is an interior point and ℓ is differentiable there, solve U(θ) = 0 for candidate values.

1. Write the support and parameter space. 2. Construct L(θ). 3. Take log L(θ). 4. Differentiate and solve the score equation. 5. Check second derivative or compare values. 6. Check boundaries and parameter restrictions. 7. State the MLE and any requested transformation.

blocks.h: Why the score equation is not the whole method
blocks.body: The maximum may occur at an endpoint, the likelihood may be monotone, a root may be a minimum, or the support may depend on θ. A solution of U(θ)=0 is only a candidate.

scenes.title: Worked example — estimate a Bernoulli probability
scenes.objective: Find an MLE from first principles, with every algebra step shown.
scenes.problem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be iid Bernoulli(p). The observed sample contains r successes and n−r failures. Find the MLE of p.

steps.say: Write the probability of one observation.
Multiply the contributions because the observations are independent.
Take logarithms to make differentiation easier.
Differentiate and set the score equal to zero.

steps.math: r(1−p) = p(n−r)  ⇒  r = np  ⇒  p̂ = r/n

scenes.after: The MLE is the observed proportion of successes. The result also makes intuitive sense: the estimated success probability should match the fraction of successes in the sample. If r=0 or r=n, the maximum is at the boundary p=0 or p=1 respectively; the endpoint check still matters.

ask.q: If 7 successes are observed in 10 Bernoulli trials, what is the MLE of p?
ask.nudge: Divide the number of successes by the sample size.

scenes.title: Pause and retrieve
scenes.objective: Check the central ideas before adding more examples.
scenes.intro: Try each answer before reading the explanation.

items.q: What is fixed when maximising the likelihood?
items.a: The observed data are fixed; the parameter varies.

items.q: Why does maximising log L give the same MLE as maximising L?
items.a: The logarithm is strictly increasing, so it preserves the location of the maximum.

items.q: Does U(θ)=0 prove that θ is the MLE?
items.a: No. It gives an interior stationary candidate. Check whether it is a maximum and inspect boundaries and parameter restrictions.

items.q: Is a likelihood a probability distribution for θ?
items.a: No. It need not integrate to one over the parameter space.

scenes.title: Worked example — exponential rate
scenes.objective: Practise a continuous likelihood and a common transformation.
scenes.problem: Let X₁,…,Xₙ be iid exponential with rate λ > 0 and density f(x;λ)=λe^(−λx), x>0. Find the MLE of λ and the MLE of the mean 1/λ.

steps.say: Write the likelihood using all observations.
Use invariance for the mean μ = 1/λ.

scenes.after: The rate MLE is the reciprocal of the sample mean, while the mean MLE is the sample mean. The rate estimator is biased upward for finite n, so do not confuse maximum likelihood with unbiased estimation. For n>1, E[n/ΣXᵢ] = nλ/(n−1).

ask.q: If n=5 and the sample total is 20, find λ̂ and the MLE of the exponential mean.
ask.nudge: λ̂ = n/total; the MLE of the mean is its reciprocal.

scenes.title: Invariance, normal variance and boundary cases
scenes.objective: Handle the three high-frequency traps: transformed parameters, n versus n−1, and parameter-dependent support.

blocks.body: If θ̂ is an MLE of θ, then for ψ=g(θ), the MLE of ψ is g(θ̂), under the induced likelihood convention. This is why a transformed target usually does not require a fresh maximisation.

blocks.h: Normal model with both parameters unknown
blocks.body: For iid N(μ,σ²), maximising the likelihood jointly gives μ̂=x̄ and σ̂²=(1/n)Σ(Xᵢ−x̄)². The unbiased sample variance is s²=(1/(n−1))Σ(Xᵢ−x̄)². They are different estimators: the MLE divides by n.

blocks.h: Uniform(0,θ): the maximum is at the boundary
blocks.body: For iid U(0,θ), L(θ)=θ⁻ⁿ when θ≥X₍ₙ₎ and zero otherwise. On the feasible region θ≥X₍ₙ₎, θ⁻ⁿ decreases as θ increases. Therefore the maximum occurs at the smallest feasible value: θ̂=X₍ₙ₎. There is no interior score root to find.
If the question asks for θ², exp(−2θ), 1/θ or another function, transform the MLE. For example, if θ̂ is the MLE, the MLE of exp(−2θ) is exp(−2θ̂), not −2exp(−2θ̂).

Under suitable regularity conditions, MLEs are often consistent and asymptotically normal, and are asymptotically efficient. These are not unconditional guarantees for every model. In particular, parameter-dependent support can violate the usual regularity conditions.

scenes.title: Your turn — Poisson maximum likelihood
scenes.objective: Complete the derivation without being shown each algebra step.
scenes.problem: X₁,…,Xₙ are iid Poisson(λ), with observed total Σxᵢ = 18 and sample size n=6. Find λ̂ and the MLE of P(X=0).

blank.prompt: Write ℓ(λ), omitting constants that do not depend on λ.
accept: sum x log lambda - n lambda
blank.hint: The product of e^(−λ) terms gives e^(−nλ); the powers of λ combine to λ^(Σxᵢ).
The score is (Σxᵢ)/λ − n. Set it to zero and rearrange.
For a Poisson variable, P(X=0)=e^(−λ). Substitute the MLE λ̂=3.

scenes.after: The estimates are λ̂=18/6=3 and P̂(X=0)=e^(−3)≈0.0498. The invariance step is just substitution into the function of λ.

scenes.title: Six statements — decide true or false
scenes.objective: Catch common MLE misconceptions before the mastery test.
scenes.intro: Give every statement a verdict before reading why.

items.claim: A likelihood function must integrate to one over all possible values of θ.
items.why: False. A likelihood is not a probability distribution over the parameter.

items.claim: Maximising the log-likelihood gives the same maximiser as maximising the likelihood.
items.why: True. Logarithm is strictly increasing on positive values.
False. The exponential rate MLE and normal variance MLE are finite-sample biased.

items.claim: If the score equation has no solution, no MLE can exist.
items.why: False. A maximum can occur at a boundary, as for Uniform(0,θ).

items.claim: The MLE of σ² in a normal model with unknown μ divides the residual sum of squares by n.
items.why: True. The n−1 divisor gives the unbiased sample variance, not the MLE.

items.claim: Under suitable regularity conditions, the MLE is often asymptotically normal.
items.why: True. The regularity qualification matters; it is not a universal finite-sample claim.

scenes.title: What you should now be able to do unaided
scenes.objective: Close the lesson with a repeatable exam method.
body: Start with the support and parameter space. Then write the likelihood as a product of the sample contributions.
Take logarithms, differentiate, solve the score equation and check the second derivative.
Inspect endpoints and restrictions. A boundary maximum may exist even when the score equation has no root.
Use invariance for a function of the parameter. Transform the MLE, do not differentiate the transformation.
Remember the standard results: Bernoulli p̂=x̄; Poisson λ̂=x̄; exponential rate λ̂=1/x̄; normal variance MLE uses divisor n.
Do not claim unbiasedness automatically. Large-sample properties require suitable regularity conditions.
The mastery test uses the existing 20-item inference_t4_mastery pool. Complete it without hints and review every explanation.
